text: ABSTRACT: Selectivity control is a very challenging topic in catalytic oxidations of alcohols using oxygen as an oxidant. Of particular interest is the catalytic aerobic lactonization of diols; due to the selectivity issue referring to the two hydroxy groups, the reaction afforded a mixture of isomeric products. Herein, we report an efficient catalytic recipe of easily available earth-abundant metal catalysts  \mathrm { F e } ( \mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ) _ { 3 } { \cdot } 9 \mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } and  \mathrm { F e C l } _ { 3 } together with TEMPO for the highly selective aerobic oxidative
section: Dual Iron-Catalyzed Selective Aerobic Lactonization of 1,6-Diols

text: lactonization of 1,6-diols, affording a variety of ε-caprolactones. The reaction was conducted under mild conditions with an O2 balloon or under ambient air enjoying high chemo- and regioselectivity for the oxidative lactonization of non-symmetric diols by the subtle recognition of the steric environment of the two hydroxy groups. Furthermore, reduction and selective aerobic oxidative lactonization constitute a formal carbonyl walking over the ε-caprolactones. Mechanistic experiments reveal a process with a hemiacetal as the intermediate. This protocol unlocks an efficient pathway to derive monomers for polycaprolactones.

text: Lactones are very common structural units in natural products and essential building blocks in organic synthesis.1,2 Especially, ε-caprolactones are indispensable monomers in the production of polycaprolactones (PCLs),3 which have been widely applied in drug-delivery systems and medical devices such as sutures and wound dressings (Scheme  1 \mathsf { a } ) . ^ { 4 } On this basis, the incorporation of functional groups into the PCL can help tune the hydrophilicity, bioadhesion, and biodegradation rate.5,6 In principle, there are two approaches to the synthesis of ε-caprolactones: the Baeyer−Villiger oxidation of symmetric cyclohexanones7,8 and oxidative lactonization of 1,6-diols (Scheme 1b).9 2- and 4-Functionalized caprolactone monomers are the most prevailing.10,11 Thus, highly selective aerobic preparation of differently substituted non-symmetric caprolactones is of current interest and high demand. The traditional approaches utilized at least stoichiometric amounts of oxidants.12−28 Thus, aerobic oxidation using oxygen would, in principle, provide a highly competitive alternative for environmental concerns. However, up to now even the formation of the parent ε-caprolactone from 1,6-hexandiol is challenging because of the unfavorable enthalpic and entropic effects of the ring.4,29−34 Remarkable catalytic recipes have been developed by Shimizu,27 Kara,35 Liu and  \mathrm { Z h u } , ^ { 3 0 } \ \mathrm { J i } , ^ { 3 6 } Backvall,̈ 3 7 Li,38  \mathrm { L i } , ^ { 3 8 } Gawande and Zboril,̌ 39 Zhou,40 and their coworkers, affording the parent ε-caprolactone from the parent 1,6-hexandiol. In addition, aerobic oxidative lactonization of non-symmetric primary  ^ { 1 , 6 } -diols with steric discrepancy remains elusive since all of the known catalytic recipes forming a mixture of isomeric lactones34,36,37,40,41 and other oxidative byproducts including ol-als and dials.18,21,24 Inspired by our early study on the  { \mathrm { F e } } ( \mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ) _ { 3 } – \mathrm { T E M P O } -cocatalyzed aerobic

oxidation of primary alcohols,  ^ { 4 2 - 4 6 } we explored the oxidation of the parent 1,6-hexandiol under our previously reported conditions combining  \mathrm { F e ( N O _ { 3 } ) _ { 3 } { \cdot } 9 H _ { 2 } O / \dot { T } E M P O / \dot { K } C l ^ { \hat { 4 } 3 } } and observed that it disappointingly afforded the desired ε- caprolactone in merely 1% yield by NMR, together with 9% NMR yield of 1,6-hexandial (Scheme 1c). Here, we wish to report the development of a new set of catalytic recipes for the highly chemo- and regioselective aerobic oxidative lactonization of 1,6-diols under mild reaction conditions, while successfully addressing the challenge of regioselectivity (Scheme 1d).

As already stated, our group reported the iron nitrate-catalyzed approaches for aerobic oxidation of alcohols by applying different cocatalysts.42−46 However, only a trace of ε- caprolactone 2a and 11% yield of 1,6-hexandial 3a was formed in the reaction of 1,6-hexandiol 1a upon using  \mathrm { F e } ( \mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ) _ { 3 } . { \mathrm { 9 H } } _ { 2 } { \mathrm { O } } , , TEMPO, and NaCl (Table 1, entry 1) as catalysts. These results prompted us to identify new cocatalysts. To our delight, after comprehensive screening, we observed that the aerobic oxidation of 1,6-hexandiol 1a with  \mathrm { B i C l } _ { 3 } as the cocatalyst afforded a mixture of ε-caprolactone 2a (53% yield),
dial 3a (18% yield), and bimolecular alcohol with an acetal unit 4a (22% yield) (Table 1, entry 2).

When 15 mol % of NaCl, which matched the stoichiometry of chloride in the used BiCl , was applied, 4% yield of ε- caprolactone 2a, 14% yield of 3a, and 24% yield of 4a were formed with 41% recovery of 1a (Table 1, entry 3). These results excluded the possibility that chloride ions alone could improve the catalytic efficiency. The structure of the bimolecular product 4a was firmly established by an X-ray crystallographic study of 4ac after copper-catalyzed aerobic oxidation47 and the subsequent reaction with 2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazine. When the loading of catalysts was reduced to 3 mol % each of  \mathrm { F e } ( \mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ) _ { 3 } { \cdot } 9 \mathrm { \check { H } } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { \mathstrut } , TEMPO, and  \operatorname { B i C l } _ { 3 } , \ \varepsilon - caprolactone 2a was obtained in 70% yield with 6% yield of 4a (Table 1, entry 4). We then screened various TEMPO

derivatives with no better results (Table 1, entries 5−7). The solvent screening indicated that the oxidation proceeded almost completely in chlorinated solvents such as DCM,  \mathrm { C H C l } _ { 3 } , and PhCl with a much poorer selectivity (Table 1, entries 8−10). Subtle adjustments of the loading of TEMPO to 2 mol % and running the reaction at  3 5 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } for 24 h afforded the product in a similar yield (Table 1, entry 12).

We next executed an intensive optimization of the cocatalysts for  \mathrm { F e ( N O _ { 3 } ) _ { 3 } } { \cdot } 9 \mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } { \cdot } \mathrm { T E M P O } combination. The alkaline metal salt MgCl was not suitable (Table 1, entry 13). To our surprise, AlCl and FeCl performed well, forming ε- caprolactone 2a in ∼ 70% yield (Table 1, entries 15 and 16). We also conducted the reaction with 9 mol % NaCl instead of 3 mol % FeCl . However, only a trace of ε-caprolactone 2a was obtained (Table 1, entry 17). In view of the cost and practicability, we chose  \mathrm { F e C l } _ { 3 } as the optimal cocatalyst. The reaction may also be conducted under ambient air with a 65% yield of 2a (Table 1, entry 18).

With the optimized conditions in hand (Table 1, entry 16), we first examined the scope of symmetric 1,6-diols (Scheme 2). A 20 mmol scale reaction of  ^ { 1 , 6 } -hexandiol 1a afforded 1.44 g (63%) of 2a. Aerobic oxidative lactonization of diols 1b−1f with the biphenyl unit afforded lactones 2b−2f exclusively in excellent yields,26,27,34,40,41 and the electron-donating methyl group and electron-withdrawing groups of chloro, fluoro, and nitro at  ^ { 4 , 4 ^ { \prime } } or  { \boldsymbol 5 } , { \boldsymbol 5 } ^ { \prime } ′-position of biphenyl were compatible. ortho-Phenyl-tethered diol 1g could also facilely undergo this transformation to deliver lactones  { \bf 2 9 } . .

The selectivity issue arises upon using non-symmetric diols: for ortho-phenyl-tethered diol 1h, benzyl alcohol was oxidized to afford the lactone 2h. The reaction of diol 1i with a highly hindered tertiary alcohol unit afforded lactone 2i in 52% yield as expected. Surprisingly, a remarkable selectivity was observed even for oxidative lactonization of 2-monosubstituted diol  { \bf i j } , affording 5-substituted lactone 2j as the major product (60% yield), while only an 8% yield of the isomeric 2-substituted

lactone  2 \mathbf { j } ^ { \prime } was formed, indicating a subtle steric preference of the less sterically hindered hydroxy group for this catalytic recipe. In the literature,34,36,37,40,41 such diols with a small steric difference for the hydroxy group led to the formation of a mixture of lactone products. Such a steric effect has been further enforced with 2,2-disubstituted diols  \mathbf { 1 k - 1 n } , delivering the corresponding 5,5-disubstituted lactones 2k−2n exclusively in good to excellent yields. Synthetically versatile ester, cyano, and bromo and potentially useful trifluoromethyl are well tolerated. Since these 2-substituted diols were prepared from the reduction of 2-substituted lactones with  \mathrm { L i A l H } _ { 4 } , this transformation to 5-substituted lactones realized a formal twostep carbonyl group ring walking over the caprolactones, affording 5-monosubstituted lactones 2o−2q in high regioselectivity and  ^ { 5 , 5 } -disubstituted lactones 2r−2C exclusively. Functional groups such as methoxy (2u), terminal C−C triple bond (2y), non-terminal C−C triple bond (2z and 2A), benzyl (2B), and C−Br bond (2C) are all compatible. Notably, chiral diols (S)-1v and (R)-1v could be smoothly transformed to optically active lactones (S)-2v and (R)-2v without racemization.

To demonstrate the necessity of each cocatalyst, some control experiments were carried out. No ε-caprolactone 2a was formed in the absence of TEMPO or  \mathrm { F e } \left( \mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } \right) _ { 3 } { \cdot } 9 \mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } (Scheme 3a, entries 2 and 3), and only a 2% yield of hexandial 3a was formed without FeCl (Scheme 3a, entry 4), proving that each catalyst was indispensable in this oxidative lactonization. Thus, two plausible reaction pathways were proposed, as shown in Scheme 3b. We assumed that the initial oxidation of 1,6-hexandiol 1a would give 6-hydroxyhexanal  { \mathfrak { s a } } , which may be transformed to 6-hydroxyhexanoic acid 6a and then esterified to furnish ε-caprolactone 2a (Scheme 3b, path a). Alternatively, 6-hydroxyhexanal 5a may also undergo intramolecular 1,2-addition to afford hemiacetal 7a with the assistance of  \mathrm { F e C l } _ { 3 } , serving as the Lewis acid to activate the carbonyl unit (path b), which would be further oxidized to form ε-caprolactone 2a. Surprisingly, the treatment of 6- hydroxyhexanal 5a48 u  { \pmb { 5 } } \mathbf { a } ^ { 4 8 } nder the standard conditions afforded ε- caprolactone 2a in only 13% yield, with 21% of dial 3a, 25% of acetal-alcohol  { \bf 4 a } , and 2% recovery of 5a (Scheme 3c, eq 1). We speculated that the in situ loading of catalysts with respect to the intermediate 5a under the standard conditions was much higher than that in eq 1 of Scheme  3 \mathsf { c } . Thus, the amount of each cocatalyst was increased up to 6 mol % of  \mathrm { F e } ( \mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ) _ { 3 } . { \mathrm { 9 H } } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } , , 4 mol % of TEMPO, and 6 mol % of FeCl (Scheme 3c,

eq 2), and the reaction of 5a smoothly gave 2a in 64% yield with 20% of dial 3a. On the other hand, 6-hydroxyhexanoic acid 6a was prepared49 on purpose and treated under the standard conditions (Scheme 3c, eq 3). However, only a 5% yield of lactone 2a was observed with 65% yield of 5- formylvaleric acid 8a. Therefore, 6a could at least be ruled out as the major intermediate here. In addition, acetal 4a could also be converted to 2a and hexandial 3a with a catalyst loading close to the reaction conditions (Scheme 3c, eq 4), indicating the easy interconversion between hemiacetals 7a and 4a. These results demonstrated that the oxidative lactonization proceeded through path b with hemiacetal 7a as the key intermediate.

Functionalized PCLs have been synthesized by ring-opening polymerization of corresponding caprolactone monomers.3 Given that the reported caprolactone monomers feature 2- and 4-substituted functional groups,10,11 we attempted to make full use of the current approach for new caprolactones with untapped potential. Fortunately, 5-substituted caprolactone 2D could be obtained through the oxidative lactonization of diol 1D with an excellent selectivity (Scheme 4). The deprotection of 2D was successfully achieved to form the non-symmetric caprolactone 8 with a free hydroxy group. Further functionalization of 8 afforded compound carboxylate 9 with 2- bromoisobutyryl bromide, benzyl ether 10 with benzyl bromide, and carboxylate 11 with pivalic anhydride, respectively. It is worth noting that the symmetric homologue of 2D (compound  2  { \mathbf { D } } ^ { \prime } ) ^ { 5 ^ { \otimes } } and the isomers of 9−11 (compounds  \hat { \mathbf { 9 ^ { \prime } } } - \mathbf { 1 1 ^ { \prime } } ) ^ { 5 1 - 5 3 } have been applied as the building blocks of PCL. We expect that our strategy may pave the way for the synthesis of new caprolactone monomers and functionalized polymers.

In summary, the catalytic recipe of  \mathrm { F e } \left( \mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } \right) _ { 3 } { \cdot } 9 \mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } / \mathrm { T E M P O } / \mathrm { F e C l } _ { 3 } was developed for the highly selective synthesis of ε- caprolactones via the aerobic oxidative lactonization of  ^ { 1 , 6 - } diols with an  \mathrm { O } _ { 2 } balloon or under ambient air. The presence of an additional catalytic component of  \mathrm { F e C l } _ { 3 } is critical for the reactivity and regioselectivity control. We reasoned that the addition of FeCl may have formed a bulkier catalyst, differentiating two types of sterically different hydroxyl groups. Combining the reduction with  \mathrm { \bar { L i A l H _ { 4 } } } and the current oxidation, formal carbonyl walking from 2-mono- or  ^ { 2 , 2 ^ { \prime } - } - disubstituted caprolactones to 5-mono- or  { \sf S } , { \sf S } ^ { \prime } -disubstituted caprolactones was realized. Non-symmetric new caprolactones may manifest the potential of this method in materials science.

General Procedure for Iron-Catalyzed Selective Aerobic Lactonization of 1,6-Diols. To a Schlenk tube were added FeCl (5.1 mg, 0.03 mmol), TEMPO (0.02 mmol),  \mathrm { F e } ( \mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ) _ { 3 } { \cdot } \mathrm { \bar { 9 } H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } (0.03 mmol), 1,6-diol 1 (1.0 mmol), and DCE (5 mL). The resulting mixture was then stirred at 35  ^ \circ \mathrm { C } under the atmosphere of  \mathrm { O } _ { 2 } from a balloon until completion of the reaction, as monitored by TLC, filtered through a short column of silica gel eluted with ethyl acetate (25 mL × 3), and concentrated. The resulting mixture was dissolved in 5 mL of MeCN, stirred with a saturated aqueous solution of NaHSO (10 mL) for 2 h, diluted with 10 mL of  \mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } , extracted with ethyl acetate  \left( 1 5 \mathrm { m L } \times 3 \right) , and dried over anhydrous  { \mathrm { N a } } _ { 2 } { \mathrm { S O } } _ { 4 } . After filtration and evaporation, the residue was purified by column chromatography on silica gel to afford the corresponding lactone 2.
